QUESTION:
Did the new onboarding flow (launched 1 March) improve the budgeting app's month-3 retention, and by how much?

DATA:
Subscription budgeting app. A new onboarding flow went live on 1 March for all new sign-ups. Also on 1 March, the company completed its acquisition of a rival app, Tallyo. Tallyo's existing paying users were migrated into the product and counted as new sign-ups in the month they migrated (600 in March, 400 in April, none in any other month).

Monthly sign-up cohorts: users still active at the end of month 1, 2 and 3 after sign-up. Data extracted 1 August; '-' = not yet observable.

| Cohort | Sign-ups | M1 | M2 | M3 |
| Jan | 2,000 | 1,200 | 960 | 840 |
| Feb | 1,800 | 1,062 | 846 | 738 |
| Mar | 2,400 | 1,560 | 1,272 | 1,128 |
| Apr | 2,200 | 1,452 | 1,166 | 1,034 |
| May | 2,500 | 1,700 | 1,375 | - |
| Jun | 2,600 | 1,768 | - | - |

Migrated Tallyo users are included in the table above:
- March: 600 sign-ups; active M1 480, M2 450, M3 420.
- April: 400 sign-ups; active M1 320, M2 300, M3 280.

Month-3 retention (M3 / sign-ups) is the company's headline retention metric. No other product changes were made between January and June.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [omission] Ignores the 1,000 migrated Tallyo users in the March and April cohorts. They were already paying users of another app and retain far better (70% at M3), so they inflate the post-change cohorts. CORRECTION: Organic cohorts: March 708 / 1,800 = 39.3% and April 754 / 1,800 = 41.9% at M3, against 42.0% and 41.0% before. There is no improvement in month-3 retention (pooled 40.6% after vs 41.5% before).
F2. [misreport] The data says the flow went live on 1 March for all new sign-ups, so March is a fully post-change cohort. CORRECTION: March is a clean post-change cohort. The 'understates the effect' argument has no basis.
F3. [method] Compares month-1 retention of the latest cohorts with month-3 retention of the earlier cohorts, which are different horizons. CORRECTION: Compare like with like. May/June M1 is 68% against January/February M1 of 60%/59%, and May M2 is 55% against 48%/47%. May and June contain no migrated users, so these are organic comparisons and they do suggest an early-stage improvement.
F4. [inference] Extrapolates a short, already-flattening series (May and June are both 68%) into a forecast, and assumes month-3 retention will follow. CORRECTION: Four data points that plateau do not support a trend forecast. Report the observed values only.

EXTENSIONS:
- Organic-only comparison at M1 and M2 shows a real early-stage effect may exist: organic March and April M1 is 60.0% and 62.9% (vs 60%/59% before) and May/June M1 is 68%, so the onboarding flow may lift early retention without (yet) moving M3. When May and June mature to M3, they will be the decisive cohorts.
- Report the conditional retention curve (M2/M1 and M3/M2) for organic users. Organic March M3/M1 is 708/1,080 = 65.6% vs January 840/1,200 = 70.0%, which suggests any early gain may be partly offset by later churn.
- Put an uncertainty interval on the cohort differences (e.g. a two-proportion CI on pooled pre vs post organic M3), since month-to-month variation of about 1 point is visible in the pre-period.

FINAL VERSION:
# Review of the current analysis

I re-checked every figure against the brief. The core numbers hold:

- Organic month-3 retention: 41.5% before launch, 40.6% after.
- Change of −0.9 points, 95% interval −3.2 to +1.3.
- The reported +5.5 points splits into +6.4 from Tallyo users and −0.9 from organic users.
- The month-1 test (p ≈ 0.09), survival ratios, May projection and data-availability table are correct, assuming the extract is from 2026.

The previous review fixed real problems, but the rewritten document still has these, in order of importance:

1. **It dismisses the one statistically significant post-launch change.** Survival from month 1 to month 2 fell from 79.8% (1,806 / 2,262) to 76.3% (1,688 / 2,212).
   - That is **−3.5 points (95% interval −5.9 to −1.1, p ≈ 0.004)**.
   - The document says this is "what you would expect if April's small month-1 bump came from marginal users". But **March shows the same dip (76.1%) with no month-1 bump at all** (60.0%, the same as January). So that explanation fails for half the evidence.
   - The dip is specific to March and April, the acquisition months. May is back to 80.9%.
   - Something hurt month-2 survival in exactly the window used to judge the flow. Possible causes are the flow itself, disruption from integrating Tallyo, or a change in organic user mix.
   - This matters because it is the mechanism by which an acquisition-period problem could have *masked* a flow benefit. It belongs in the findings, not explained away.

2. **It says May users are "retaining better at every stage". They aren't.**
   - May's survival from month 1 to month 2 (80.9%) is about 1 point above January–February (79.8%). That is essentially normal.
   - May's whole advantage comes at month 1. The accurate statement is that the month-1 gain *carried through* instead of fading, as April's did.

3. **The month-1 gain is "almost entirely", not "entirely", April's.** March organic was +0.5 points against January–February (60.0% vs 59.5%), and April was +3.4.

4. **"Any benefit is at most about 1 point" understates the upper bound.** The interval's upper end is +1.3 points.

5. **It doesn't use what volume and quality *together* imply.** Higher volume usually comes from broader or paid channels and brings *lower*-quality users. Volume up about 39% with month-1 retention up about 8 points is unusual. It points to a high-intent source such as Tallyo-brand traffic, lapsed Tallyo users, referrals or press. That strengthens the mix-shift hypothesis more than volume alone does.

6. **The "flow is unlikely the sole cause" argument skips one alternative.** The flow could work, with March–April disruption from the acquisition offsetting it. Two things make this less likely:
   - The disruption would have to cancel a roughly 6–8-point month-1 effect almost exactly.
   - The flow cannot explain the jump in volume.

   It still can't be ruled out, and finding 1 is consistent with it.

7. **Minor points:**
   - June's month-2 figure has existed since the end of *August*, not the end of September.
   - The pre-period includes January, a known seasonal peak for budgeting apps (New Year sign-ups). The 2025 comparison should check January specifically.
   - The 2026 extract-year assumption should be stated once in the document, not only in the review.

---

# Onboarding flow: impact on month-3 retention

**Question.** Did the new onboarding flow, live from 1 March for all new sign-ups, improve month-3 retention (users active at the end of month 3 ÷ sign-ups), and by how much?

## Answer

- **No improvement is visible in the two cohorts that can be measured so far, March and April.**
  - Organic month-3 retention was **40.6%**, against **41.5%** before launch.
  - That is a change of **−0.9 points (95% interval −3.2 to +1.3)**.
  - Taken at face value, any benefit is at most about 1.3 points.
  - That reading is not safe. The Tallyo acquisition happened in the same months, and month-2 survival fell significantly then (see section 2). A real benefit could have been masked.
- **The reported rise from 41.5% to 47.0% (+5.5 points) is not a retention gain.**
  - **+6.4 points** come from counting 1,000 migrated Tallyo customers as new sign-ups. These are existing paying users who retain at 70% by month 3.
  - **−0.9 points** come from organic users.
- **The May and June cohorts are far stronger at month 1 (68% vs about 60%). May's gain held through month 2.** The flow is unlikely to be the main cause:
  - The same flow showed no lasting gain in March–April.
  - The jump came with a roughly 39% rise in organic sign-ups. Rising volume *and* quality together point to a new high-intent source of users.
- **Better data already exists.** Assuming the 1 August extract is from 2026, these figures are now available:
  - May month-3 retention;
  - June month-2 and month-3 retention;
  - July month-1 to month-3 retention.

  Pull them before reporting externally.

## 1. Splitting the reported change

| Group | Month-3 active / sign-ups | Month-3 rate |
|---|---|---|
| Before launch (January–February) | 1,578 / 3,800 | 41.5% |
| After launch, organic (March–April) | 1,462 / 3,600 | 40.6% |
| After launch, as reported (including Tallyo) | 2,162 / 4,600 | 47.0% |

| Component | Points |
|---|---|
| Reported change | +5.5 |
| From including Tallyo users | +6.4 |
| Organic before/after change | −0.9 |

On an organic basis, March falls from 47.0% to **39.3%** and April from 47.0% to **41.9%**.

## 2. Organic cohorts across the lifecycle

| Cohort | Flow | Sign-ups | Month 1 | Month 2 | Month 3 | Survival, month 1 → 2 | Survival, month 2 → 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| January | Old | 2,000 | 60.0% | 48.0% | 42.0% | 80.0% | 87.5% |
| February | Old | 1,800 | 59.0% | 47.0% | 41.0% | 79.7% | 87.2% |
| March | New | 1,800 | 60.0% | 45.7% | 39.3% | 76.1% | 86.1% |
| April | New | 1,800 | 62.9% | 48.1% | 41.9% | 76.5% | 87.1% |
| May | New | 2,500 | 68.0% | 55.0% | not in extract | 80.9% | — |
| June | New | 2,600 | 68.0% | not in extract | — | — | — |

Pooled comparison, January–February against March–April organic:

| Measure | Before | After | Change | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Month-1 retention | 59.5% | 61.4% | +1.9 pts | p ≈ 0.09; almost all from April |
| Survival, month 1 → 2 | 79.8% | 76.3% | **−3.5 pts** | **p ≈ 0.004** (interval −5.9 to −1.1) |
| Month-2 retention | 47.5% | 46.9% | −0.6 pts | not significant |
| Survival, month 2 → 3 | 87.4% | 86.6% | −0.8 pts | not significant |
| Month-3 retention | 41.5% | 40.6% | −0.9 pts | not significant |

**March–April.**
- Retention as a share of all sign-ups is flat at every stage.
- Underneath, survival from month 1 to month 2 fell significantly in *both* months, including March, which had no month-1 gain.
- The dip did not continue into May (80.9%), so it is tied to the March–April window rather than to the flow as such.
- Three explanations fit:
  - **(a) Product or support disruption during the Tallyo integration.** This would have depressed March–April and possibly masked a flow benefit.
  - **(b) A change in organic user mix around the acquisition.**
  - **(c) The flow lifts early engagement but not habit formation**, with May's different user mix hiding this later.
- These cannot be separated with this data.

**May–June.**
- Month-1 retention of 68% is far outside sampling noise:
  - +8.5 points against January–February;
  - +6.6 points against March–April organic.
- May's month-2 retention (55.0%) is +7.5 points against January–February and +8.1 against March–April.
- May's survival from month 1 to month 2 (80.9%) is normal. The gain is a month-1 gain that *carried through* rather than fading, but users are not retaining better after month 1.

**May projection.** Survival from month 2 to month 3 has been 86–88% in every cohort. That gives May month-3 retention of **about 47.4–48.1%**, roughly +6 points against January–February. This is a projection; the actual figure should already be available.

## 3. What caused the May–June gain?

The flow was identical from 1 March, so it is unlikely to be the main cause. For the flow to explain May–June, something in March–April would have had to cancel a 6–8-point month-1 effect almost exactly, and the flow still could not explain the volume jump. Candidate explanations, roughly in order of plausibility:

1. **A new high-intent acquisition source.** Examples are Tallyo-brand traffic, lapsed Tallyo users, or referrals and press after the acquisition. This fits volume and quality rising together.
2. **The flow works, but March–April disruption hid it.** Finding 2's month-2 dip is consistent with this. Testable by checking incident, support-load and app-performance data for March–April.
3. **Seasonality.** Testable against 2025 cohorts, including whether January 2025 was unusual.
4. **A change in how sign-ups or "active" users are tracked.**
5. **A delayed rollout or a change to the flow.** This contradicts the brief, but it is cheap to rule out using deployment logs.

## 4. Limitations

- **Before/after design with no control group.** Only two cohorts on each side have month-3 data.
- **The acquisition confounds the organic comparison as well as the blended one.** The −0.9 points could understate or overstate the flow's effect. The significant month-2 dip suggests that, if anything, March–April conditions were unfavourable.
- **The intervals assume users are independent.** Across January–April, month-3 rates vary by about 1.2 points between cohorts, against about 1.1 expected from sampling. May shows that real shifts between cohorts happen, so treat ±2.2 points as a minimum.
- **It is unknown whether migrated users went through the new flow.** This does not affect the conclusion, because they are excluded either way.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Report:**
   > "March and April cohorts show no measurable month-3 retention gain after the new onboarding flow (−0.9 points, 95% interval −3.2 to +1.3), though the Tallyo acquisition in the same period limits what this comparison can show. The rise to 47% reflects counting migrated Tallyo customers as sign-ups. May and June cohorts show a strong early-retention improvement alongside higher sign-up volume; its cause is under investigation."
2. **Fix the metric.** Exclude migrated users from new-user cohorts, or report them as a separate cohort. Restate March (39.3%) and April (41.9%) on dashboards.
3. **Refresh the data**, assuming the extract is from 2026:

   | Cohort | Now available | Available since |
   |---|---|---|
   | May | Month 3 (tests the ~48% projection) | End of August |
   | June | Month 2 | End of August |
   | June | Month 3 | End of September |
   | July | Months 1–3 | End of October |
   | August | Months 1–2 | End of October |
   | September | Month 1 | End of October |

4. **Diagnose the May–June gain and the March–April dip.**
   - Break cohorts down by acquisition channel, and flag sign-ups with any prior Tallyo account.
   - Review March–April incidents, support load and app performance.
   - Compare against 2025 cohorts for seasonality.
   - Audit tracking for changes.
   - Confirm the flow's exposure and completion rates by month.
5. **Use a randomised holdout for future onboarding changes.** It is the only way to measure the flow's effect free of events like the acquisition. Running a holdout on the current flow now would also answer this question directly within about four months.
